'''''Gomphrena globosa''''', commonly known as '''globe amaranth''', is an edible plant from the family [[Amaranthaceae]]. The round-shaped flower [[inflorescence]]s are a visually dominant feature and cultivars have been propagated to exhibit shades of magenta, purple, red, orange, white, pink, and lilac. Within the flowerheads, the true flowers are small and inconspicuous.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Jiang|first1=Yifan|last2=Zhao|first2=Nan|last3=Wang|first3=Fei|last4=Chen|first4=Feng|date=2011-01-01|title=Emission and Regulation of Volatile Chemicals from Globe Amaranth Flowers|journal=Journal of the American Society for Horticultural Science|language=en|volume=136|issue=1|pages=16–22|issn=0003-1062|doi=10.21273/JASHS.136.1.16|doi-access=free}}</ref>

''Gomphrena globosa'' is native to Central America including regions Panama, and Guatemala, but is now grown globally.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Roriz|first1=Custódio Lobo|last2=Barros|first2=Lillian|last3=Carvalho|first3=Ana Maria|last4=Santos-Buelga|first4=Celestino|last5=Ferreira|first5=Isabel C.F.R.|title=Pterospartum tridentatum, Gomphrena globosa and Cymbopogon citratus: A phytochemical study focused on antioxidant compounds|journal=Food Research International|language=en|volume=62|pages=684–693|doi=10.1016/j.foodres.2014.04.036|year=2014|hdl=10198/10145|url=https://bibliotecadigital.ipb.pt/bitstream/10198/10145/4/To_FRI_Revised.pdf|hdl-access=free}}</ref> As a tropical annual plant, ''G. globosa'' blooms continuously throughout summer and early fall. It is very heat tolerant and fairly drought resistant, but grows best in full sun and regular moisture.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Silva|first1=Luís R.|last2=Valentão|first2=Patrícia|last3=Faria|first3=Joana|last4=Ferreres|first4=Federico|last5=Sousa|first5=Carla|last6=Gil-Izquierdo|first6=Angel|last7=Pinho|first7=Brígida R.|last8=Andrade|first8=Paula B.|title=Phytochemical investigations and biological potential screening with cellular and non-cellular models of globe amaranth (Gomphrena globosaL.) inflorescences|journal=Food Chemistry|language=en|volume=135|issue=2|pages=756–763|doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2012.05.015|pmid=22868155|year=2012}}</ref> The plant fixes carbon through the [[C4 carbon fixation|C<sub>4</sub> pathway]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Herold|first1=A.|last2=Lewis|first2=D. H.|last3=Walker|first3=D. A.|date=1976-05-01|title=Sequestration of Cytoplasmic Orthophosphate by Mannose and Its Differential Effect on Photosynthetic Starch Synthesis in C3 and C4 Species|journal=New Phytologist|language=en|volume=76|issue=3|pages=397–407|doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.1976.tb01475.x|issn=1469-8137|doi-access=}}</ref> At maturity, the flowerheads are approximately {{convert|4|cm|in}} long and the plant grows up to {{convert|24|in|cm}} in height.<ref name=":0" />

''Gomphrena globosa'' is an outcrossing species that is pollinated by butterflies, bees, and other insects. Floral volatiles likely play a significant role in the reproductive success of the plant by promoting the attraction of pollinators.<ref name=":0" />

==Uses==
In [[Hawaii]], it is commonly used in long-lasting [[Lei (Hawaii)|lei]]s since it retains its shape and color after drying.

In [[Nepal]], the flower is known commonly as ''makhamali ful'' and is used to make a garland during [[Tihar_(festival)|Bhai Tika]], last day of [[Tihar (festival)|Tihar festival]]. The garland is put around the brother's neck by their sister for protection. The slow withering character of the flower symbolizes a long life for the brother. The flower was included in the gift sent to [[United Kingdom|Britain]] by [[Jung Bahadur Rana]] in 1855. This flower is known as ''Rakta Mallika'' in [[Sanskrit]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=संवाददाता |first=सफल खबर |title=मखमली फूलको सांस्कृतिक महत्व |url=https://www.safalkhabar.com/news/16808 |access-date=2022-06-22 |website=www.safalkhabar.com |language=Nepali}}</ref>

This plant is common in landscape design and cutting gardens for its vivid colors and color retention.

The edible plant ''G. globosa'' has been used in [[herbal medicine]].<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite book|title=Cote ce Cote la: Trinidad & Tobago Dictionary|author=Mendes, John|date=1986|location=[[Arima]], Trinidad|page=7}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lans|first=Cheryl|date=2007-03-15|title=Ethnomedicines used in Trinidad and Tobago for reproductive problems|journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine|volume=3|pages=13|doi=10.1186/1746-4269-3-13|pmid=17362507|pmc=1838898|issn=1746-4269 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Medicinal and Aromatic Plants VI|last=S.|first=Bajaj, Y. P.|date=1994|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|isbn=9783662303719|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|oclc=840292441}}</ref>

The flowers of ''G. globosa'' are rich in [[betalain|betacyanins]] which have a wide range of applications as additives and supplements in the food industry, cosmetics, and livestock feed. Stable between pH 3 and 7, the betacyanins in globe amaranth are well suited to be used as natural food dye and have a red-violet color.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Roriz|first1=Custódio Lobo|last2=Barros|first2=Lillian|last3=Prieto|first3=M.A.|last4=Morales|first4=Patricia|last5=Ferreira|first5=Isabel C.F.R.|title=Floral parts of Gomphrena globosa L. as a novel alternative source of betacyanins: Optimization of the extraction using response surface methodology|journal=Food Chemistry|language=en|volume=229|pages=223–234|doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2017.02.073|pmid=28372168|year=2017|hdl=10198/14894|url=http://bibliotecadigital.ipb.pt/bitstream/10198/14894/1/Roriz%2cC.L_Floral-parts-of-Gomphrena2017.pdf|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

==Chemical properties==

=== Phytochemicals ===
At least twenty-seven [[phytochemical]]s have been detected in ''G. globosa'' including six phenolic acid derivatives and fifteen specific flavonoids. The most abundant phenolic compounds present are [[flavonoid]]s. A major phenol was found to be kaempferol 3-O-rutinoside based on chromatographic and mass spectrometry techniques.<ref name=":1" /> Gomphrenol derivatives also contribute to phenolic content. Other flavanols include [[quercetin]], [[kaempferol]], and isorhamnetin derivatives.<ref name=":2" />

=== Betacyanins ===
The major betacyanins identified in globe amaranth are gomphrenin, isogomphrenin II, and isogomphrenin III.<ref name=":1" /> These compounds are stored in vacuoles in the plant.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tanaka|first1=Yoshikazu|last2=Sasaki|first2=Nobuhiro|last3=Ohmiya|first3=Akemi|date=2008-05-01|title=Biosynthesis of plant pigments: anthocyanins, betalains and carotenoids|journal=The Plant Journal|language=en|volume=54|issue=4|pages=733–749|doi=10.1111/j.1365-313X.2008.03447.x|pmid=18476875|issn=1365-313X|doi-access=}}</ref>

=== Volatiles ===
Cultivars of ''G. globosa'' vary in the identity of floral volatiles but the volatile compounds of nonanal, decanal, geranyl acetone, and 4,8,12-tetradecatrienal, 5,9,13-trimethyl, were commonly detected by chromatography-mass spectrometry analysis. The cultivar ‘Fireworks’ has a high abundance of volatile esters such as geranyl propionate, geranyl isovalerate, benzyl isovalerate, and benzyl tiglate. The floral volatile emission of this cultivar of ''G. globosa'' was found to exhibit a diurnal pattern independent of light. Emission of floral volatiles can be regulated by phytohormone and defense signaling molecules. Experimentally, the ethylene inhibitor silver thiosulphate increased volatile emission of molecules derived from the terpenoid pathway. Defense signaling molecules can have temporal effects on floral volatile emission such as increased emission after four hours and reduced emission of volatiles after 24 hours in time studies analyzed with chromatography-mass spectrometry.<ref name=":0" />
